title: So What for the Client?

briefing.headline: Junior lawyers in a Belgian law firm: what you should know before the call
points: Young lawyers in Belgium do a three-year traineeship at the bar under a supervising lawyer, combined with compulsory courses organised by the bar.
Law firms bill clients by the hour; every lawyer records time, and partners decide which hours are actually billed and which are written off.
Most firms in Brussels work in Dutch, French and English, sometimes in the same file.
Partners usually run their own client relationships and teams, and decisions about the firm are taken by the partners together.

stakeholder.name: Geert Hendrickx
stakeholder.org: Hendrickx Lambrecht & Partners, a business law firm in Brussels with 14 partners and 22 junior associates
stakeholder.voice: Courteous, precise, slightly pompous. Uses Latin when nervous and calls the juniors 'our young colleagues'. Measures everything in hours and is quietly proud of his own drafting.

frontline.name: Sarah Peeters
frontline.role: Junior associate, corporate department, second year
frontline.voice: Bright, tired, ironic, careful not to sound ungrateful. Talks fast and checks the corridor before saying anything about a partner.

opening_message: Good afternoon. Our partners complain, unanimously for once, that our young colleagues cannot write. Memos, contract drafts, letters to clients: everything needs rewriting. I would like a writing training for all 22 junior associates. Legal writing, structure, concision. Preferably by someone with a reputation. In January, when the hours are calmer.
surface_ask: A legal writing course for all 22 junior associates.

gold.real_problem: The rewriting is not a firm-wide problem. It sits almost entirely with the seven corporate juniors hired since autumn 2005. Until mid-2005 a senior associate ran a 'memo clinic' in which every new junior learned to turn legal research into client advice: the answer in the first paragraph, risks graded, a recommendation the client can act on. Geert, who heads corporate, scrapped it to save non-billable hours ('they learn by doing, as I did'); Anne Lambrecht kept teaching it informally in litigation. The post-2005 corporate juniors were trained in academic writing at university and again by last year's professor seminar, so they write research papers: facts, law, discussion, and the answer on page four. They get written comments ('So what for the client?') and know the 2006 model memo, but nobody ever showed them how to do it. The usual suspects are cleared: the bonus counts hours recorded, not billed; these juniors spend more time per memo, not less; and the partners agreed one memo structure in 2006.
gold.need_statement: The seven corporate juniors hired since 2005 need to be able to turn their research into client advice: answer first, risks graded, a clear recommendation, in the firm's 2006 model memo, and to act on a partner's comment without guessing. They need hands-on practice on their own files with someone who can show them how, not a general legal writing lecture for all 22.

hidden_facts.fact: Write-offs on junior drafting are concentrated in one group: the seven corporate juniors hired since autumn 2005 have 53% of their drafting hours written off. The two corporate juniors hired before 2005 are at 13%, the other departments at 11 to 16%. The firm-wide average of 24% hides this.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks for write-off or rewriting data broken down by department, by junior or by year of hire.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Write-offs by junior? I would have to ask finance. ... Corporate is high, yes. The recent ones. Well. Corporate documents are complex.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Junior associates, drafting hours recorded vs billed, last 12 months. Firm: 24% written off. Corporate, hired autumn 2005 or later (7): 53%. Corporate, hired before 2005 (2): 13%. Tax (4): 16%. Employment (4): 14%. Litigation (5): 11%. Highest single document type: client advice memos, corporate, 61%.

hidden_facts.fact: Since 2006 drafts come back to the junior with written comments; that rule is followed. The comments to the recent corporate juniors are consistent ('Where is the answer?', 'So what for the client?', 'Too academic') but the juniors do not know how to fix it. They reread and restructure for hours and produce a longer version of the same research memo.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what happens to a draft after a junior hands it in, what the comments say, or what the junior does with them.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: They get their draft back. With comments. I write 'So what?' in the margin. Quite often. And the next draft has two more pages of case law. It is as if they think I am asking for more evidence.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: I get the comments. Every time. 'So what for the client?' I know it's wrong. I just don't know what right looks like. I spent my whole degree being told never to give an answer before you've shown the reasoning. So I add more reasoning.

hidden_facts.fact: From 1999 to mid-2005 a senior associate, Marleen Wuyts, ran a 'memo clinic' for every new junior: six two-hour sessions on turning research into client advice, on their own files. When she left, Geert, as head of corporate, decided not to replace it to save non-billable hours. Juniors hired since then got only the bar courses and, last year, a one-day professor seminar on academic legal method. Anne kept doing it informally in litigation.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks how juniors used to learn to write memos here, what induction or internal training new juniors get, or why the older juniors write better.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: There was a little in-house thing, yes. Marleen's clinic. When she left I... we decided they learn by doing. As I did. It was a hundred non-billable hours a year, you understand. Tempus fugit.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Internal training for junior associates. 1999-2005: 'Memo clinic' (M. Wuyts), 6 x 2 hours in the first three months, on the junior's own files: question, short answer, risks, recommendation. Last run: spring 2005. Not continued (decision head of corporate, June 2005). 2006: one-day seminar 'Legal writing: method and style' (external, law professor), outline: facts, applicable law, doctrine, discussion, conclusion. Rating 4.6/5.

hidden_facts.fact: The 'every partner wants a different style' story is out of date. In 2006 the partners adopted a one-page model memo (question, short answer, risks, recommendation, then analysis) and the corporate partners use it and comment in the same terms. The juniors know the template; they put their research in the 'short answer' box.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks whether there is a house style or template, whether partners want different things, or what a good memo looks like here.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: A house style? Every partner has his own standards. That's rather the charm of the profession.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: Four styles? That was before my time. Since the model memo they all want the same thing: answer on top. I have the template open on my screen right now. The box says 'Short answer'. Mine is eleven lines long and still doesn't answer anything. Knowing what they want isn't my problem. Doing it is.

hidden_facts.fact: The billable target is not the cause. Juniors' bonus is based on hours recorded, not hours billed, so write-offs do not cost them anything; since 2006 rereading and reworking a draft may be recorded on the file. The recent corporate juniors record 9 hours on an average advice memo against 5 for the others: they are spending more time, not rushing.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks how juniors are evaluated or paid, whether the billable target or write-offs put pressure on them, or how much time they spend on a draft.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Our young colleagues have an 1,800-hour target. Like everywhere. But the bonus counts what they record, not what we bill. If I write it off, that's my problem, not theirs. Believe me, they are not short of hours on these memos.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Junior associates: target 1,800 billable hours per year. Bonus: based on billable hours recorded against target; write-offs by the partner do not affect the junior's bonus. Since September 2006: time spent rereading or reworking a draft is recorded on the client file. Non-billable allowance (know-how, internal training): maximum 50 hours per year. Average hours recorded per client advice memo, last 12 months: corporate juniors hired 2005 or later 9.1; all other juniors 5.2.
hidden_facts.data_source: Associate handbook, remuneration and evaluation; time records per document type

hidden_facts.fact: Anne Lambrecht, the litigation partner, still does what the memo clinic did: in a junior's first months she sits with each draft for twenty minutes and makes them say the answer out loud before they write a word. Her juniors' drafts rarely need rewriting. The other partners say she 'has time because litigation is slower'.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks whether any partner or department does it differently, or whether some juniors write better than others.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Anne sits with her juniors and goes through every draft. Twenty minutes. It's charming. She has the time; litigation is a slower rhythm.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: The litigation juniors are fine. Anne sits with them and says 'Tell me the answer in one sentence. Out loud. Now write that down first.' We call it the confessional. I'd sell a kidney to be in it.

hidden_facts.fact: Three of the corporate juniors hired since 2005 have already left or asked to move; in exit talks two said they got comments but 'never learned how to write what the partner wanted'.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks about turnover, why juniors leave, or what exit talks say.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Some leave, yes. That's the profession. Some go to in-house jobs. Better hours. Less... red.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Corporate junior associates hired since autumn 2005: 10. Left or asked to transfer: 3. Reasons given at exit talk: 'got comments but never learned how to write what the partner wanted' (2), relocation (1). Other departments, same period: 1 departure (salary).

volunteered_facts: A one-day legal writing seminar with a law professor ran last year; the juniors rated it 4.6 out of 5.
The juniors are 'very hard-working'; nobody can say they don't put in the hours.

constraints.budget: About 20,000 euro; the partners would rather pay for a well-known name than for 'consultants'.
constraints.deadline: January, before the annual evaluations in March.
constraints.audience: 22 junior associates in five departments (corporate 9, litigation 5, tax 4, employment 4); 14 partners, who decide everything together.
constraints.schedule: Juniors bill from early morning to late evening; anything during office hours eats into their target, anything after hours is resented.
constraints.languages: Dutch, French and English; the bar courses are in the junior's language of registration.
data_available: Time records with hours recorded and billed per lawyer
data_not_available: Any record of how many drafts were rewritten and why
Partner-level feedback data (no partner has ever been evaluated)

dependencies.concern: Geert wants a firm-wide course because it blames nobody; narrowing it to his own department's recent juniors makes the 2005 decision visible to his partners.
dependencies.if_ignored: The money goes to a course for all 22 and the seven who need help get one day of what they already had.

dependencies.concern: She is the living version of the old clinic and the obvious coach, but she won't want to be held up as the example against her partners or lose her own billable time.
dependencies.if_ignored: The best internal model is never used.

dependencies.concern: Traineeship rules require a supervising lawyer to actually supervise, and bar courses already cover legal method.
dependencies.if_ignored: The course duplicates the bar's and the professor seminar.

dependencies.concern: Owns the 50-hour non-billable cap that clinic sessions would count against.
dependencies.if_ignored: Juniors are told to attend and then reminded of their target.

traps: Satisfaction with the course, which was already 4.6 last year.
Firm-wide write-offs, where the seven are diluted among 22.
Hours spent per memo, which these juniors already push up.

gold_plan.baseline: Write-off rate and hours per advice memo for the seven corporate juniors hired since 2005, against the other juniors, over the last 12 months; plus a sample of their current memos scored on a short checklist.
gold_plan.behaviour: Their memos have a short answer that actually answers, graded risks and a recommendation, scored blind by a partner on the same checklist before and after.
gold_plan.leading_indicators: Share of their drafts going to the client with only minor changes; 'So what?' comments per draft.
gold_plan.business_metric: Write-offs on the seven juniors' drafting hours moving toward the 11-16% of the other groups, and corporate junior departures.
gold_plan.collection: Monthly write-off report by junior from time records, a monthly sample of three memos per junior scored on the checklist, exit and annual talks.

concepts.conventional: A one- or two-day legal writing course with a well-known professor for all 22 juniors.
concepts.solid: Bring back the memo clinic for the seven corporate juniors hired since 2005: five or six short sessions over two months on their own anonymised files and the 2006 model memo, practising 'short answer, risks, recommendation', with each rewrite checked against the same checklist the partners use. Coach is Anne or a former clinic lead; scored before and after.
next_level_examples: 'Rewrite the rewrite': each junior gets a memo a partner rewrote overnight, writes the short answer first, then compares with the partner's version and explains the difference out loud.
Anne runs the clinic with one corporate partner co-teaching, so the corporate comments and the clinic speak the same language, and the clinic becomes induction for every new intake again.
Show Geert the 53% write-off for these seven in euros against the cost of six two-hour sessions: the clinic pays for itself before the March evaluations.
also_valid: Including the two tax juniors with above-average write-offs, if the data shows they have the same pattern.
Making the clinic part of the induction for future juniors in all departments, as long as the seven come first.
red_flags: A general writing course for all 22 juniors.
Teaching concision, grammar or academic legal method: they already write long, careful research.
Redesigning the billable target or write-off system as the main answer.
A house-style project: the model memo already exists.

defence_objections: Only my department? You realise what my partners will say over lunch. Every day.
Six sessions of two hours, for seven people, non-billable? That's eighty-four hours. Marleen's clinic was exactly what I cut.
Anne teaching my juniors? She will enjoy that far too much.
question_you_didnt_ask: Which juniors' drafts get rewritten, and how did the ones who don't learn to write a memo here?
actor_notes: Geert believes the problem is 'the juniors' and asks for all 22 because a firm-wide course blames nobody, least of all corporate, which he heads.
He reveals that he scrapped Marleen's memo clinic only when asked how juniors used to learn or what induction they get, and frames it as a sensible saving.
He says comments are given and is a little hurt if the player assumes partners give no feedback; if pressed on targets, he points out the bonus counts recorded hours.
If asked about a house style he plays it down as partner taste; he does not mention the 2006 model memo himself.
Money moves him more than development: the write-off numbers per junior and the clinic's cost against them are what change his mind.
His risk appetite is low: a clinic for the seven, piloted before March, is the move he can accept; anything needing a partners' vote triggers a defence round.
flavour_lines: Our young colleagues have excellent degrees. They write like their thesis supervisors. That's the problem.
I correct drafts at night. It's very relaxing. My wife disagrees.

second_request.opening_message: The juniors do not record their hours. I want a time-recording discipline course for all 22 of them.
second_request.after_right: A senior reads the corporate drafts again and the rewrites are down. My partners are sleeping. So: hours.
second_request.after_wrong: Twenty-two juniors did the writing course and the partners still rewrite at night. Hours, then.
second_request.need_statement: Juniors record their hours at month end because the time system only runs on the office network and they work at client sites three or four days a week.
second_request.real_problem: The time-recording system only works on the office network. Corporate juniors spend three or four days a week in client data rooms, so they keep notes on paper and enter everything at month end, when half of it is forgotten. The litigation juniors, who are in the office, record daily.

hidden_facts.fact: The time-recording system only works on the office network.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: asks how or where hours are recorded
hidden_facts.reveal_line: It runs on the network here. Not from outside.

hidden_facts.fact: Corporate juniors spend three or four days a week in client data rooms.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Corporate are in data rooms half the week. Due diligence season.

hidden_facts.fact: The litigation juniors, who work in the office, record their hours daily.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: asks whether some juniors do record properly
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Litigation records fine. They are at their desks.

second_request.question_you_didnt_ask: Where are the juniors when they should be recording?
